tip: Dari Sabang sampai Merauke = 'all across Indonesia' – Sabang is the country's far western tip, Merauke its far eastern one. The set phrase for the whole nation.
The me- prefix can turn a noun into a verb: laut (sea) becomes melaut, to head out to sea – which is what nelayan (fishermen) do every morning.
Ber- can mean 'having': gunung berapi is literally a mountain having api (fire) – a volcano. The fire is built right into the word.
Pasar kaget is literally a 'startled market' – it appears in a lapangan or street out of nowhere and is gone again within hours.
A complaint like this shrinks in speech to noun + -nya + a comment: Nyamuknya banyak, ya! = so many mosquitoes, huh. The pattern works with any noun.
Pak RT is the elected head of the Rukun Tetangga, the smallest neighborhood unit – a real official, and the person everyone in the kompleks knows.
Padahal flags a surprising contrast – 'even though / when in fact': takut kecoak, padahal berani memegang ular. Scared of the small thing, brave with the big one.
Pasang here means high tide: air laut pasang = the tide is in. It's the same word as pasang 'install/set up' – context tells you which one you've got.
Kami mohon pengertian... is the fixed apology formula of announcements – airports and stations use it word for word. Language you'll hear far more than speak.
Turun tangan is literally 'lower a hand' – to step in personally. The manajer turun tangan when he finally comes down and handles it himself.
Buah tangan is literally 'hand fruit' – a small gift you bring back from a trip. It's the polite word; in everyday speech you'll mostly hear oleh-oleh.
Indonesian gives opinions with 'according to me': menurut saya = in my opinion. Menurut works for any source – menurut dia, menurut berita.
Sempat before a feeling marks it as momentary: sempat bingung = got confused for a bit. The feeling came and then passed.
Saja comes after the phrase it limits – lima menit saja, not saja lima menit. The reverse of English 'just five minutes'.
Demi is a formal 'for the sake of': demi keselamatan bersama = for our shared safety. Announcements and oaths use it; casual speech just says untuk.
Paling lambat is literally 'at the slowest', and it means 'at the latest': konfirmasi paling lambat hari Jumat – the deadline phrase of letters and forms.
Commands drop the me- prefix: forms say lampirkan (attach), not melampirkan. Any me-...-kan verb loses me- when it becomes an instruction.
Dilarang + verb is the sign formula for 'No ...-ing': dilarang berjualan = no selling. Swap in another verb and you can read most street signs.
Signs speak formally: pengunjung dilarang membawa makanan. Said aloud, the same rule is just tidak boleh bawa makanan – the formal noun dropped, membawa clipped to bawa.
Termasuk is literally 'entered (into the group)' – masuk with ter-. Termasuk anak-anak means the children are counted in: 'including'.
Nggak jadi = 'ended up not happening': jadi means 'materialize', so nggak jadi pindah says the move was planned and then fell through.
Mendingan is spoken 'better (to)': mendingan kita ke pantai = better we hit the beach. Casual only – in writing you'd see lebih baik.
Doubling kapan (when) blurs it: kapan-kapan = 'sometime', no date attached. Kapan-kapan kita coba kafe baru = we should try that new cafe sometime.
Gara-gara means 'because of' with blame attached: gara-gara hujan deras, the rain gets the fault for the soaked shoes. Neutral cause is karena.
Seumur hidup = se- (one) + umur (age) + hidup (life): 'one lifetime'. Berlaku seumur hidup means the KTP never expires.
Beliau is the respectful he/she for elders and officials: beliau sedang dinas luar. Using dia for a lurah would sound too casual.
Dilegalisir names a real ritual: getting official stamps on copies of your ijazah so they count as true copies. Job and school applications demand it.
Ber- + a noun can mean going to get it: obat (medicine) gives berobat, to seek treatment. Tempat berobat = the place you go to get treated.
Antara lain introduces a partial list – 'among others': syarat antara lain akta kelahiran dan kartu keluarga means those plus more not named.
Cair is literally 'liquid'; for money it means paid out: THR ayah cair = Dad's bonus came through. Salaries and funds cair when they land.
Mohon maaf lahir dan batin is the fixed Lebaran formula: 'forgive my wrongs, outward and inner' – lahir is the outward side, batin the inner.
The angpao rule: married adults give the red envelopes, the unmarried receive – which is why the card says belum menikah. Marriage flips your role.
Cuti bersama is government-set shared leave glued onto a holiday – the whole kantor closes on those dates whether you asked for leave or not.
The birthday custom runs in reverse: yang berulang tahun wajib mentraktir – the birthday person treats everyone else, not the other way around.
-kan can mean 'have it done': periksa = examine, periksakan ke dokter = have it examined by a doctor. You arrange the action, someone else performs it.
Semoga cepat sembuh is the standard get-well line, literally 'hopefully quickly recover'. Semoga starts most wishes: semoga sukses, semoga lancar.
News and clinics shorten demam berdarah to DBD – three-letter abbreviations are everywhere in Indonesian, from KTP to SD.
Anak kos means a boarding-house renter, and it connotes a tight budget: masakan anak kos = cheap cooking. Hence memasak sendiri at the end of the month.
An arisan is a rotating savings club: everyone pays in each round, one member takes the whole pot, and the rotation runs until all have had a turn.
Sembako is short for sembilan bahan pokok – the nine staple goods (rice, oil, sugar and so on). Harga sembako = the price of the basics everyone tracks.
Ujung means 'end'; doubled, ujung-ujungnya is literally 'at its very ends' = 'it always ends up': ujung-ujungnya penuh barang yang tidak penting.
Chili prices swing constantly and everyone tracks them – harga cabai naik lagi? is genuine national small talk at any market stall.
Demi builds 'X by X' phrases: sedikit demi sedikit = little by little, satu demi satu = one by one. The doubling marks slow, steady progress.
Kena means 'get hit by' something unwelcome: kena biaya = get charged a fee, kena hujan = get rained on, kena macet = get stuck in traffic.
On its own, tukang means a handyman – the tukang with his palu and gergaji. Add a trade and it names the specialist: tukang kayu = carpenter.
